Video encoding is mostly used because the space requirements for raw video are impossible to tolerate on today's technology. A 1920x1080 film running at 24fps yields 1920 * 1080 * 24 * 24 bits of data per second. The first 24 is from 24 bits per pixel. The second from 24 frames per second. That's a total of about 149 megabytes per second. You'd need a 1200 Mbps internet connection to stream uncompressed 24 fps 1920x1080 video. You can more than double that for 60fps video. Quadruple it for 4k video. And so on.

But at the same time look at things that we used to not be able to transmit efficiently, but now can. Even things like plain text used to be often zipped back in the day when downloading a megabyte was a coffee break event. Now we just send it in plain text because it's more convenient and there's really no reason not to. In the future there's no real reason to expect encoding to really be a major thing.

Just a fun little factoid that's only tangentially related to the answer. The answer being AI systems. The thing that deep learning systems are already phenomenal at doing is taking chaos and breaking it into coherent chunks of 'stuff'. Video data, even if it requires a decryption layer, can be broken down to coherent chunks of somehow similar data. That's a dream scenario for AI. Think about the universal translator - it's the same exact business, just a whole lot easier since you have mountains of data to work with.
